new_statements.quote: Word stress is generally word-initial, though words with word-final stress are not rare. Word stress can in some words shift from word-final to word-initial, and vice versa, e.g. pushi ‘cat’ occurs as pushi as well within one text (the underlined syllable is stressed [pu- vs. -shi]). This is very probably due to word stress being subordinate to sentence stress (de Josselin de Jong 1924: 9), though not much is known about sentence stress in Dutch Creole. || de Josselin de Jong 1926: 9: "Niet alleen is het woordaccent bijna volkomen ondergeschikt aan het zinsaccent, maar het phonetisch complex van het afzonderlijke woord wordt zoozeer overheerscht door de rhythmische klankenreeks van den zin, dat een phonetische beschrijving van afzonderlijke woorden en klanken slechts een gebrekkige voorstelling kan geven van het klankstelsel als geheel."
new_statements.translation: de Josselin de Jong 1926: 9: 'Not only is the word accent almost completely subordinate to the sentence accent, but the phonetic complex of the individual word is so dominated by the rhythmic sound-sequence of the sentence that a phonetic description of individual words and sounds can give only a defective picture of the sound system as a whole.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the first syllable; a sizeable class of words (many non-Dutch loans, e.g. kabá 'finish', gobét, banglá, kabái) has final stress, marked with an acute accent in de Josselin de Jong's 1926 texts; some words vacillate between initial and final stress within a text, attributed to word stress being dominated by sentence stress/rhythm.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with word-final stress 'not rare'; stress in some words shifts between final and initial (pushi 'cat'); word accent almost wholly subordinate to sentence accent, vowel quantity dependent on sentence rhythm (de Josselin de Jong 1926: 9).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is corpus-based (de Josselin de Jong's 1922-23 dictated narratives from St. Thomas/St. John speakers, stress marked with acute accent; plus Sabino's recordings of the last speaker), not instrumental; word-level default explicitly said to be overridden at sentence level. Language extinct (last speaker d. 1987).
new_statements.identity_note: Negerhollands = Virgin Islands Dutch Creole (nege1244, ISO dcr). The stress statement concerns the 20th-century spoken variety of St. Thomas and St. John as recorded by de Josselin de Jong in 1922-23 (nine elderly speakers) and by Sabino in the 1980s (last speaker), not the 18th-century missionary 'Hoch Kreol' written register. No separate glottocode for these varieties.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work (Hesseling 1905) was listed, so a second silent work to spot-check does not exist. Spot-check of Hesseling went beyond the reader's chapters: I downloaded the remaining DBNL sections not held by the project (Voorbericht, Verklaring der verkortingen, Bloemlezing A Taalproeven van Pontoppidan pp. 129ff, B texts from G.D., C texts from G.H., and the Woordenlijst pp. 273ff) and searched them for the Dutch and German stress vocabulary: nothing about stress or accent anywhere. Bloemlezing D-F (NT and Psalm texts, ch0013-0018) were not downloaded; they are scripture translations and carry no grammatical commentary. Nothing missed.
